eventSummary.en: After Jesus ascended, the apostles returned to Jerusalem and waited together. Matthias was chosen by lot to complete the Twelve, and on the day of Pentecost they were all together in one place.

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to pray for the new believers there. This atlas marks Samaria at the Shechem and Mount Gerizim region.

display.en: Earlier in c. AD 30, with the Twelve

eventSummary.en: On the day of Pentecost, James was with the apostles in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That day about three thousand people were baptized.
Herod Agrippa I, moving against the church, had James the brother of John killed with the sword in Jerusalem. Acts records no journey for him beyond this city.
On the day of Pentecost, John was with the apostles in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That day about three thousand people were baptized.
The apostles sent Peter and John to Samaria. They prayed for the believers there, and the believers received the Holy Spirit. This atlas marks the region at Shechem and Mount Gerizim.

display.en: Earlier, c. AD 70, before the island

eventSummary.en: Eusebius preserves the tradition that John lived and taught at Ephesus. Acts does not send him there.

disputes.en: The New Testament does not place the apostle at Ephesus. The tradition comes through second-century writers as Eusebius reports them.

eventSummary.en: Revelation's author says he was on the island of Patmos “for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ.” Whether this John is the apostle is disputed.

disputes.en: Revelation 1:9 names John on Patmos and does not call him the son of Zebedee. Early tradition identifies them. Some scholars do not.

display.en: Later, c. AD 98, the tradition of his death

eventSummary.en: The same tradition brings John back to Ephesus after Patmos and places his death there.

disputes.en: A return to Ephesus and a death there are church tradition reported by Eusebius, not a statement of Acts or Revelation.

eventSummary.en: On the day of Pentecost, Andrew was with the apostles in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That day about three thousand people were baptized.

display.en: Earlier, c. AD 50, the tradition of Scythia

eventSummary.en: Eusebius, citing Origen, says Scythia was allotted to Andrew. The source names a region, not a town, so the pin is Pontic Olbia, a Greek city on that coast.

disputes.en: Acts does not send Andrew to Scythia. Eusebius reports a tradition and names no city. Olbia is a real Black Sea coordinate in that region, not a place the ancient notice identifies.

display.en: Later, c. AD 60, the tradition of his death

eventSummary.en: Later church tradition says Andrew was crucified at Patrae in Achaia. Eusebius' allotment names Scythia, not this city.

disputes.en: The New Testament and Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History 3.1 do not name Patrae. The crucifixion there is later tradition, reported as such.

eventSummary.en: On the day of Pentecost, Philip the apostle was with the apostles in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That day about three thousand people were baptized. He is not the Philip who preached in Samaria and met the Ethiopian.

display.en: Later, c. AD 80, the tradition of his burial

eventSummary.en: Eusebius quotes Polycrates of Ephesus: Philip, one of the Twelve, “sleeps in Hierapolis.” Proclus, also quoted by Eusebius, places a tomb of Philip and his daughters there. Eusebius notes that the Philip of Acts at Caesarea is the evangelist.

disputes.en: Polycrates calls the Philip at Hierapolis one of the Twelve. Luke's Philip with four prophesying daughters is the evangelist at Caesarea. Eusebius sets the two notices side by side. This stop follows Polycrates and does not use Acts 8.

display.en: Earlier in c. AD 30, with the eleven

eventSummary.en: Bartholomew is named among the eleven who stayed in the upper room in Jerusalem after the ascension. There they prayed together with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.
On the day of Pentecost, Bartholomew was with the apostles in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That day about three thousand people were baptized. No later city is marked.
On the day of Pentecost, Thomas was with the apostles in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came upon them. That day about three thousand people were baptized.

display.en: Later, c. AD 70, the tradition of Parthia

eventSummary.en: Eusebius, citing Origen, says Parthia was allotted to Thomas. The source names a region, not a town, so the pin is Hecatompylos, a Parthian royal city.

disputes.en: Acts does not send Thomas to Parthia. Eusebius reports a tradition. Hecatompylos is one Parthian capital, not a city he names. A later India story is not pinned here.

display.en: Earlier in c. AD 30, chosen by lot

eventSummary.en: The believers in Jerusalem put forward Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias. They prayed, cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, who was numbered with the eleven apostles.
Matthias, newly numbered with the apostles, was with them in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost. That day about three thousand people were baptized. No later city is marked.
